title: Elijah Goes First
by: for Elijah, on his August birthday

vocab.kidDefinition: bugs that sit up in the trees and buzz all afternoon when it's hot
a cat with soft dark stripes and sometimes a small M-shape on her forehead
Kinley's word for seeing a thing one second before it happens
the big rolling sound the sky makes after a flash of lightning
the shape all the tall buildings make against the sky
did a thing over and over until it started to get easier

pages.text: Elijah's birthday came on a Friday in the middle of August. It was the kind of afternoon when summer sits on Atlanta like a big warm dog. The city had been waiting on rain that would not come. The sidewalks were hot. The cicadas would not hush.

Elijah was the one who went first. First out the door, first foot in the pool, first hand up when somebody needed somebody. His big sister Kinley was nine. Kinley's braids had beads on the ends that clicked when she turned her head, and she watched everything.

Down at the corner where the big oak leaned over the sidewalk. A small crowd of grownups was looking up and pointing. Somebody's tabby cat had gotten herself up onto the highest branch and could not get down. She was crying.

Elijah looked up. He looked around at the grownups, all of them talking about calling somebody. Then he started climbing.

"Baby, come down from there," somebody said. "We're going to call the fire truck."

But Elijah was already three branches up. The branches were getting farther apart. His knees were finding things to scrape. He kept going.

At the top he found two things.

One was the tabby, warm and shaking, with a small green collar and no name tag.

The other was a plain black baseball cap. Wedged deep in a branch fork. Dusty with leaves. Like it had been up there a long time, waiting.

Coming down was harder than going up. He came down anyway, cat under one arm, cap in the other hand.

A woman on the sidewalk with worried eyes took the tabby back. She cried a little and thanked him about six times. She did not ask about the cap.

Nobody did. So it was his.

chapters.title: The Half Power and the Reveal

pages.text:
Out back by the fence, Elijah put the cap on. It sat down over his eyebrows. He bent his knees and jumped.

He went up as high as a mailbox and came down laughing.

He tried it again to make sure. Same thing. Higher, even. He landed on his heels, out of breath, still laughing.

Then he ran inside to tell Kinley.

Kinley was on the couch with a book. She looked up at him and did not look surprised.

She held out her hand.

On the end of one braid, a single bead had gone completely still.

"I've had mine a long time," she said.

"I get a longsight," she said. "I see a thing about a second before it happens, and my beads go still. Then it happens. But seeing it isn't the same as getting there in time. I try, Elijah. I never get there."

Elijah thought about that.

"So you see," he said. "And I go."

Kinley's beads clicked, three of them at the same time, like a small round of applause.

They practiced all week on small things. A cup going over the edge of the table — Kinley saw, Elijah went. A dog loose on Ponce. A red balloon getting away from a girl outside the market. Small ones. Every single one of them small.

chapters.title: The Storm and the Cat Again

pages.text: On Saturday the rain finally came, and it came all at once. Uncle Manav and Auntie Indira had driven down from New Jersey. Little Azi was with them, small enough to still get carried. They were all on a picnic blanket in Piedmont Park when the sky went the color of a plum.
Thunder walked across the park, slow and enormous. And then the lights of Atlanta went out, block by block. The streetlights. The market. The whole gold skyline, gone like somebody pulling a zipper.

Over by the biggest oak, a small girl was crying. Her tabby — the same tabby, the same green collar — had bolted up the trunk when the thunder started.

Kinley took a step toward the tree. Her beads did not go still. She stopped.

"I can't see her, Elijah. It's too dark."

Kinley started climbing anyway. She got about as high as the first big branch. Then her foot slipped in the wet, and she stopped, both hands on the trunk.

"Okay," she said. "Okay."

Elijah put on the cap. He said the thing they had been practicing.

"You see. I go."

Then he looked up at Kinley on the branch and thought about it.

"This time I'll see too. Stay right where you are."

He went up as high as a porch roof. That is not very high for a superhero. It was exactly high enough.

He stopped at Kinley's branch first and helped her down onto the wet grass.

Then he went higher, and found the tabby wedged in a fork of the tree, wet and shaking. He tucked her inside his shirt and came down.

They came down on the blanket. The streetlights came back on all at once. The whole park went gold and dripping.

The small girl hugged her tabby about nine times. Mama got one arm around Elijah and one around Kinley, and did not let go for a while.

Later there was a bath, and dry pajamas, and the good kind of tired. The cap sat on the bedpost where he could see it.

Kinley stopped in his doorway on her way to bed. Her beads clicked twice, quiet.

"Same time tomorrow?" she said.

"Same time tomorrow," said Elijah, who had been the birthday kid for eight whole days.

The rain kept on. The dark was warm. Both of them slept.

story_core.notes: Now a proper superhero origin, not equipment-inheritance. Elijah earns the cap by acting first without powers (climbing the oak for the tabby the grownups will only call about) — the Green Lantern beat, courage before ring. Kinley's power is a reveal AFTER his, not a shy confession up front: he shows her his jump, she calmly holds out a stilled bead and says 'I've had mine a long time.' The Ch 3 rescue is deliberately low-stakes — the same tabby up another tree during the blackout, Kinley stuck on the low branch she tried to climb, Elijah lifting them both down. The moral turn (going first, without knowing it will pay off) is now the origin, not a montage.

age_fit.notes: Measured: 913 words, 20 pages, 3 chapters, 109 sentences, average 8.4 words, longest 18. Word count sits 13 above the 6-8 band's 900-word ceiling to buy the earning beat and Kinley's reveal — honestly named rather than trimmed with a hatchet. Sentence-length ceiling is clean: zero sentences over 20 after splitting the page-1 opener at 'August' and the page-3 crowd line at 'sidewalk'. Kinley is 9 and sits above the band — she is written as a character, not as the reader. Age dropped from Elijah's descriptions throughout — 'the birthday kid' rather than 'six', per buyer request.

personalization.notes: Birthday is the spine — book opens on his birthday, cap arrives that day as the one present nobody bought him, ends on 'the birthday kid for eight whole days.' Age deliberately unnamed at buyer's request. Season pinned to mid-August, day-of-month open. Personalisation callbacks intact and load-bearing: Kinley's beaded braids as the physical tell for her power, sibling dynamic played as go-first / watches (mechanical setup for 'you see, I go' — and its Ch 3 flip, 'this time I'll see too'), Atlanta heat / cicadas / Ponce / Piedmont Park / gold skyline. Godparent cameo intact — Uncle Manav, Auntie Indira, Azi at the picnic — but no longer the crisis; the rescue is a stranger's tabby, not family. That is the correct choice for a celebratory book: the family is the safe frame around the adventure, not the source of the adventure's stakes.

craft.notes: Sensory throughout — summer sitting on you like a warm dog, beads clicking and then going still, knees finding things to scrape, cap dusty with leaves. No compliment loops: nobody in the book calls Elijah brave, first, strong, or a hero at any point. The go-first trait shows only in what he does — climbing the oak while adults call for a fire truck, saying 'I go' to Kinley, going up in the dark. Nobody teaches; the closest thing to a moral is Kinley's own 'I've had mine a long time' beat, which is sibling gift rather than lesson. Ends on rain, warm dark, sleep.

family_tool.notes: parent-guide.md unchanged in spirit — The Two-Part Power (say what you see / say who goes / name it after) still applies, and it now maps even better because Kinley's power is established rather than confessed. Adult read: this is a book about acting on courage before knowing whether it will be rewarded, and about a big sister whose gift is not being upstaged by her little brother's newer one. Not a regulation tool; a coordination and mutual-witnessing frame for the 6-and-9 sibling pair.

rubric.pattern_used: authoring-doctrine.md 'When in doubt → buyer wants pure celebration' (witnessing spine, hoped_lesson as spine), restructured after buyer feedback into a proper superhero origin — courage BEFORE the object, not caused by it.
rubric.notes: Second-pass rewrite after buyer feedback: the first draft's 'reach for a hat on a counter and get powers' read as found-object, not origin. This draft moves the origin onto a first act of courage (climbing an oak for a stranger's cat while grownups call for a fire truck) and lets the cap be the consequence, not the cause. Kinley's power moves from a shy Ch-2 confession to a Ch-2 reveal AFTER Elijah's first jump — she has had hers a long time; the book was hiding a hero in plain sight. Ch 3's stakes are deliberately kept light per buyer instruction: no cousin in danger, no life-threatening scenario. A tabby up a tree during the blackout, Kinley stuck on a low branch she tried to climb, Elijah lifts them both down. Names confirmed by the buyer (Mama, Dada, Uncle Manav, Auntie Indira, tabby unnamed on purpose). Page-1 opener split at 'August' to keep every sentence in the book under 20 words, per the age-fit correction 046a831 made against v1.
